title: Section check: AI in daily life
intro: 8 questions about Lessons 9–12. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: A water office now has a machine read the forms that clerks used to type. Which word fits?

options.text: Exposure
options.feedback: Not quite. Exposure means a tool could do some tasks in a job. Here, the machine already does the work. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: Training
options.feedback: Not quite. Training means lessons that teach people new skills. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: Automate
options.feedback: Yes. To automate is to make a machine do work that people used to do.

stimulus.title: A made-up clinic job
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Bea works at the front desk of the made-up Northport Clinic. She answers the phone, books visits and helps people who feel worried. Now a new tool books most of the visits.

questions.question: Based on Lesson 9, what is most likely to happen to Bea's job?

options.text: It changes, and she does other tasks
options.feedback: Yes. The tool does one task. People are still needed for others, like helping worried people.

options.text: The tool now does every part of her job
options.feedback: Not quite. The tool books visits, but it does not help worried people. Tools often do some tasks, not a whole job. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: Nothing about her work changes
options.feedback: Not quite. The tool now does one of her tasks, so her work changes. Look back at Lesson 9.

questions.question: Bangkok is a big city. Why does it help when AI sorts the reports?

options.text: It means the city needs no workers
options.feedback: Not quite. People still check each report and fix the problem. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: It gets each report to the right office
options.feedback: Yes. A big city has many offices. Sorting sends each report to the one that should deal with it.

options.text: It makes every repair free for the city
options.feedback: Not quite. A bigger job may need money and a plan. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.question: In 2022, Traffy Fondue won a Thai government award. What does the prize show?

options.text: Officials thought it was valuable
options.feedback: Yes. A prize shows that officials valued it. It does not show how many problems were fixed.

options.text: How many problems it helped to fix
options.feedback: Not quite. A prize does not count repairs. It shows that officials valued the platform. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: That every report was fixed in time
options.feedback: Not quite. Bangkok says about 79% were resolved, not all. A prize does not show this. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.question: In the study in Nigeria, students did better on an English test. What do the researchers say led to this?

options.text: The AI tool, working all on its own
options.feedback: Not quite. Trained teachers were in the room too. The researchers say the whole programme mattered. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: Extra lessons with no computers at all
options.feedback: Not quite. The students used an AI chat tool in computer rooms. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: The tool and the teachers together
options.feedback: Yes. Teachers started each session and helped students stay on task. The tool and the teachers worked together.

stimulus.title: Two made-up students
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Dani and Kofi practise maths with a made-up homework helper. Dani asks for a hint, then solves each problem himself. Kofi asks for the full answer every time and copies it. Next week, they both take a test with no tools.

questions.question: Think of the study in Türkiye. Who will likely do better on the test?

options.text: Kofi, who copied the full answers
options.feedback: Not quite. In Türkiye, full answers became a shortcut. That group did worse on the test alone. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: Dani, who asked for hints
options.feedback: Yes. In Türkiye, the hint group did about as well as the books group. The full-answer group did worse.

options.text: Both will get the very same score
options.feedback: Not quite. In Türkiye, the hint group did about as well as the books group. The full-answer group did worse. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.question: Face recognition software turns the measurements of a face into a set of numbers. What is this set called?

options.text: A database
options.feedback: Not quite. A database is a large store of information. It can hold many faces. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: A template
options.feedback: Yes. A template is a set of numbers saved from a face. It is used to check the face later.

options.text: A match
options.feedback: Not quite. A match is when the tool estimates that two faces belong to the same person. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.question: A face search says a person in a video matches a photo in its database. What is this match?

options.text: The software's best guess
options.feedback: Yes. A match is a guess, not proof of who someone is. A wrong match can get someone blamed.

options.text: Proof of who the person is
options.feedback: Not quite. A match can be wrong. It is the software's best guess. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: A photo that the phone keeps
options.feedback: Not quite. A phone usually keeps a template, not a photo. A match is the software's best guess. Look back at Lesson 12.

results.high: Well done. You can see what AI does at work, in a city, at school and with faces, and what people still do.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 9–12, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
